strengths: Addresses a crucial and timely problem in LLM safety: the widening gap between the rapid evolution of jailbreak attacks and static, hard-to-maintain evaluation benchmarks.
Well-engineered architecture with a clear separation of concerns across the library (JBF-LIB), synthesis pipeline (JBF-FORGE), and standardized evaluation suite (JBF-EVAL).

Thorough empirical evaluation reproducing 30 distinct attacks (spanning various search dynamics and carrier formats) across 10 victim models, demonstrating strong fidelity (mean ASR delta of +0.26 percentage points).
Impressive engineering efficiency, cutting LOC by 42% compared to author repositories and achieving an 82.5% code reuse rate while keeping end-to-end translation time to under 30 minutes on average.
Comprehensive documentation in the appendix, including concrete agent prompts, audit criteria, source-of-truth priority rules, and complexity analyses.
weaknesses: Heavy reliance on reference repositories: 22 of the 30 evaluated attacks rely on official reference repositories. As shown in the ablation (Figure 2), having official code yields substantial improvements (+19.8% mean ASR over paper-only), indicating that paper-to-module synthesis remains brittle when paper descriptions omit low-level scaffolding details.

Potential judge subjectivity and bias: Standardized evaluation in JBF-EVAL relies primarily on a single LLM judge (GPT-4o), which may carry known judge-specific alignment biases and refusal-detection quirks across diverse target models.

Lack of automated regression and versioning testing in the current implementation: Although discussed in Future Work, the current system does not yet evaluate continuous automated ingestion or historical backward compatibility under continuous model/API drift.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: benchmark stagnation and reproducibility bottlenecks in LLM jailbreak research caused by the rapid pace of published attacks and manual integration overhead.

Well-designed multi-agent architecture (JBF-FORGE): The separation of responsibilities among Planner, Coder, and Auditor—governed by strict source-of-truth precedence (Plan > Contract > Reference Repo) and bounded audit loops—provides a principled framework for paper-to-code synthesis.

Substantial empirical effort: Successfully reproduces 30 recent jailbreak attacks (22 with official code, 8 from text only) and evaluates them across 10 distinct victim models under a unified harness and judging protocol.

Valuable system-level engineering contributions: Demonstrates concrete software engineering benefits via JBF-LIB, achieving a 42% LOC reduction relative to original repositories and an 82.5% shared framework reuse ratio.

Insightful cross-model analysis: The standardized 30-attack × 10-victim evaluation uncovers meaningful findings regarding attack mechanisms (e.g., formal wrappers vs. linguistic reframing) and model-specific blind spots (e.g., GPT-OSS-120B vs. commercial instruction-tuned models).
weaknesses: Misleading aggregate fidelity metric: Reporting a signed mean deviation of +0.26 percentage points masks substantial individual errors (e.g., SATA-MLM at +20.0 pp, SATA-ELP at +16.4 pp, ISA at -16.0 pp, SCP at -11.8 pp). The authors should report Mean Absolute Error (MAE) or RMSE alongside signed mean error to accurately represent reproduction fidelity.

High dependence on reference implementations: The ablation in Section 4.2 shows a large drop (-19.8 percentage points on average) when reference code is omitted. This indicates that paper text alone is often insufficient for faithful synthesis of complex scaffold-heavy attacks, qualifying the claim of autonomous 'paper-to-runnable' translation.

Evaluation protocol drift in Table 1: For several attacks, the judge or victim model had to be substituted (e.g., using GPT-4o where human evaluation or different models were originally used). While understandable from a practical standpoint, this confounds the comparison between reported and reproduced ASR.

Scope limited to black-box prompt/scaffold attacks on AdvBench: The framework primarily targets API-level black-box prompting techniques and evaluates mainly on AdvBench. It does not address white-box/gradient-based attacks (e.g., GCG) which require custom tensor operations and dedicated GPU training scaffolding.

Reliance on closed, frontier proprietary models: The synthesis pipeline depends on an ensemble of proprietary models (Gemini-3-pro, Claude-4.5-Sonnet, GPT-5.1 Codex), which may introduce reproducibility drift over time as model versions change.

strengths: Addresses a critical and timely problem in AI safety: the rapid obsolescence of static jailbreak benchmarks and the substantial engineering friction required to standardize disparate attack implementations under a common evaluation harness.

Comprehensive empirical scope: successfully evaluates 30 jailbreak attacks across 10 victim models, demonstrating strong reproduction fidelity (mean ASR deviation of +0.26 percentage points compared to published numbers in matched settings).
Effective software engineering design: JBF-LIB achieves significant implementation compression (42% LOC reduction, 82.5% shared framework reuse) via unified contracts and reusable LLM wrappers.

Insightful cross-model empirical analysis (Section 5): reveals crucial attack-model interaction dynamics, such as how search strategy effectiveness varies by model (e.g., sampling outperforming victim-loop optimization on certain models but reversing on others) and the format sensitivity of commercial vs. research models.

Transparent ablation studies: explicitly isolates the impact of having reference repositories vs. paper-only descriptions (Figure 2) and quantifies the utility of the enhanced refinement pass (Figure 3).
weaknesses: Modest algorithmic novelty: The multi-agent workflow (Planner-Coder-Auditor) is a standard domain specialization of established agentic software engineering patterns (similar to Paper2Code, LMR-Bench, and AutoReproduce) rather than a novel agentic architecture.

Heavy reliance on reference source code: While titled 'From Papers to Runnable Attacks', 22 of the 30 reproduced methods rely on official reference repositories. The ablation in Figure 2 demonstrates that without reference code, reproduction ASR drops substantially (average drop of nearly 20 percentage points on representative attacks, e.g., GTA dropping from 100% to 51.4%), indicating that the pipeline functions primarily as an automated code-porting/refactoring agent rather than a true paper-to-code synthesizer for complex methods.

Evaluation reliance on a single automated LLM judge: The standardized evaluation in JBF-EVAL relies almost exclusively on GPT-4o as a judge on AdvBench. Prior literature (e.g., HarmBench, StrongREJECT) has shown that automated LLM judges can suffer from systematic false positives or false negatives when presented with structured formats (e.g., code, JSON, math equations, or obfuscated ciphers), which could confound the carrier-format comparisons in Section 5.2.

Missing operational cost and resource characterization: Although end-to-end wall-clock time is analyzed (mean 28.2 minutes), the paper does not report financial API costs, token consumption, or failure rates across the multiple closed frontier models (Gemini-3-pro, Claude-4.5-sonnet, GPT-5.1 Codex, Claude Code) utilized in the loop.

Architectural constraints for complex interactive attacks: Standardizing attacks into a single `generate_attack` entry point returning a string works well for prompt wrappers and single-turn attacks, but may face scalability bottlenecks as attacks evolve toward dynamic multi-turn agents with environment interactions.

strengths: Addresses a crucial and timely bottleneck in LLM safety evaluation: the rapid staleness and fragmentation of jailbreak benchmarks due to inconsistent evaluation harnesses and manual integration burdens.
Extensive empirical execution: successfully reproduces 30 distinct jailbreak attacks across 10 modern LLM victim models, presenting a large-scale 30x10 cross-model evaluation matrix on AdvBench.

Rigorous multi-faceted fidelity analysis: provides not only aggregate ASR comparisons (mean delta of +0.26 pp), but also trace-level behavioral comparisons, an 8-dimension manual semantic fidelity audit, and with-repo vs. no-repo ablations.

High engineering rigor and transparency: clearly quantifies codebase compression (58% LOC reduction, 82.5% infrastructure reuse), computational overhead (time, token usage, caching breakdowns in Appendix D), and includes full agent system prompts.
weaknesses: Heavy reliance on reference code repositories: 22 of the 30 reproduced attacks rely on official reference repositories. The ablation in Section 4.2 shows that without reference code, ASR drops substantially (e.g., from 86.3% to 66.5% across 5 evaluated attacks). Thus, the framework operates largely as a repository refactoring/adaptation agent rather than purely translating papers to code.

Evaluation in the standardized benchmark (JBF-EVAL) is restricted to AdvBench and relies exclusively on a single judge model (GPT-4o). AdvBench is widely recognized to have limitations in behavior coverage and complexity, and LLM-as-a-judge backends can exhibit systematic scoring biases.

The enhanced refinement pass requires knowing the ground-truth reported ASR (`ASRpaper`) as a triggering condition (threshold tau = -10.0 pp). In a fully autonomous continuous ingestion scenario for newly released attacks or new victim models, this thresholding mechanism may not cleanly generalize without human oversight.

The core multi-agent architecture (Planner-Coder-Auditor with test/repair loop) is a relatively conventional design in the paper-to-code and code-generation literature; the primary novelty lies in domain-specific abstraction and application rather than methodological innovation in multi-agent systems.

strengths: Addresses a timely and crucial bottleneck in LLM safety research: the rapid drift and lack of reproducibility between published jailbreak techniques and static evaluation suites.

Well-engineered agentic framework: decomposing the workflow into JBF-LIB (standardized contracts and runtime scaffolding), JBF-FORGE (iterative planner-coder-auditor loop with strict precedence rules and bounded refinement), and JBF-EVAL (decoupled datasets, models, and evaluators) enforces clean separation of concerns.
Thorough and broad empirical study reproducing 30 distinct jailbreak attacks spanning multiple search strategies and carrier formats, evaluated across 10 modern victim LLMs.

Strong fidelity evaluation: beyond matching reported ASR within a mean gap of +0.26 percentage points, the authors provide trace-level comparisons, code-compression analysis, and manual semantic fidelity audits.

Extensive ablations and cost analyses, including with-repo vs. no-repo performance, enhanced refinement pass analysis, model ablation across agent roles (planner/coder/auditor), and token usage breakdowns.
weaknesses: High dependence on reference codebases: as shown in Section 4.2 (Figure 2), reproduction fidelity drops significantly without reference repositories (ASR drops by 19.8 percentage points on average on the ablated subset), showing that paper text alone is often insufficient for high-fidelity automated synthesis.

Frontier model dependency and synthesis cost: the pipeline requires top-tier proprietary models (Gemini-3-pro, Claude-4.5-Sonnet, GPT-5.1 Codex, Claude Code) and averages ~3.86M tokens per attack synthesis, which might hinder adoption for resource-constrained academic environments.

Scope is currently limited to text-based black-box and gray-box attacks evaluated primarily on AdvBench/JBB; white-box attacks, multi-modal jailbreaks, and automated defense module synthesis are left to future work.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely challenge in LLM safety: the divergence, rapid staleness, and lack of reproducibility across fragmented jailbreak research implementations.

Systematic architecture and workflow design: JBF-LIB establishes standardized base contracts and reusable scaffolding, while JBF-FORGE cleanly separates planning, coding, and static auditing with explicit source-of-truth precedence rules.

Extensive empirical execution: Successfully integrates and benchmarks 30 diverse jailbreak attacks spanning multiple search paradigms (single-pass, stochastic sampling, stateful, victim-in-the-loop) and carrier mechanisms.

Detailed ablation and diagnostic evaluation: Includes insightful analyses on the impact of reference repositories versus paper text alone (Figure 2), agent role sensitivity (Table 5), LOC compression (Table 8), and budget/token efficiency trade-offs (Figure 6).

High level of experimental transparency and reproducibility: Provides full system prompts (Figures 7–11), explicit pseudocode (Algorithm 1), trace-level comparisons, and manual semantic audit scorecards (Appendix F).
weaknesses: Over-reliance on reference repositories: While marketed as translating 'papers to runnable attacks', the ablation in Section 4.2 reveals that paper text alone results in a substantial drop in reproduction fidelity (mean ASR drops by ~19.8 percentage points on tested methods). This indicates the system primarily serves as an automated code-refactoring and harness-adapter agent rather than a true paper-to-code synthesizer.

Target ASR feedback during refinement introduces optimization-on-the-test-set concerns: In Algorithm 1 and the Enhanced Refinement Pass (Appendix L), the system evaluates the generated attack against the evaluation benchmark and triggers code modifications if ASR undershoots by >10%. Using benchmark performance to iteratively patch implementation logic risks overfitting attack parameters and prompts directly to the evaluation split.

Evaluation on AdvBench with a single automated judge (GPT-4o) has well-documented biases: Automated judges are prone to misclassifying benign refusals containing sensitive keywords or empty compliance as jailbreaks. While Appendix F conducts small-scale manual checks on four attacks, the broader cross-model benchmark (Section 5) relies strictly on GPT-4o without measuring judge agreement across diverse models.

Limited scope to text-only black-box/gray-box attacks: White-box optimization attacks (e.g., GCG) and multimodal attacks are excluded due to differing runtime requirements (logit access, non-textual carriers), which limits the universality of the current JBF-LIB abstraction.

High compute and proprietary API dependency: End-to-end synthesis requires coordinating three distinct proprietary frontier models (Gemini-3-pro, Claude-4.5-sonnet, GPT-5.1 Codex) consuming ~3.86M tokens per attack on average, raising practical accessibility barriers for environments lacking multi-provider frontier API access.
